paragraphs: Beyond the mountains, beyond the forests, beyond seven lakes, there lived three little pigs: Crunchy, Oinky, and Eusebius. Their childhood was peaceful and safe, and every day they grew a little plumper, as piglets do. But at last there came a special moment that comes to every little pig sooner or later: the time to leave Mum's home and make their own way in the world.

Before they set off, their loving mother gave them one last piece of advice. “Remember, my dear children, oink-oink. Hard work and doing things properly are the keys to a peaceful life, oink. Don't sleep too long or spend all your time playing. Do your chores with care, and good fortune is sure to smile on you, oink-oink.”
And so their mother said goodbye to her children. Even after their round little figures had disappeared over the horizon, she went on waving her white handkerchief.
Meanwhile, Crunchy, Oinky, and Eusebius marched cheerfully on. Each brother hoped to find a wonderful spot for his new home.

Crunchy took a fancy to a meadow full of flowers. Among the tall grasses, chamomile flowers, poppies, and cornflowers shimmered with colour, while cheerful birdsong invited him to dance and play. It was a beautiful place, and there Crunchy began building his house.

“I've never been very strong, so I don't fancy spending ages building, squeak-oink,” he said to himself. “I'm a rather weak little pig, and I need plenty of sleep. That haystack looks lovely. I'll make a house just like it, oink!”

No sooner said than done! He gathered all sorts of grasses and built a green-and-gold hut, with a front door made of sticks. Building it took him a whole day. Pleased with himself, he went inside his new home and fell asleep.

Crunchy's brother, Oinky, wandered into a clearing in a young wood beside a lovely little river sparkling in the sunshine. Brown, yellow, and red mushroom caps peeped shyly out of the soft moss, while marsh marigolds and water lilies covered the stream. It was a beautiful place, and there Oinky began building his house.
“I don't fancy spending too much time building, squeak-squeak,” he grunted to himself. “I don't like working. I like fishing! That beaver lodge looks lovely. I'll make a house just like it, oink!”

No sooner said than done! He gathered twigs, sticks, and branches and built a sturdy wooden hut. He made the door from some planks he had found, and even fitted a window with shutters. Building it took him three days. Pleased with himself, he dusted off his trotters and settled down to fish.
Eusebius continued his journey until he reached a place among the rocky hills.

“Well, straighten my curly tail!” he said to himself. “All this walking has worn me out. I could do with a nap or a spot of fishing. But first I must build a sturdy little house, oink-oink. As strong and unshakeable as that rock over there!”

No sooner said than done! He carried over heavy stones, mixed some mortar, and began building a house as solid as the rocks around it. He even gave it a little window and a smart chimney. For the door and shutters, he used sturdy oak planks. Building it took him three whole weeks! It was very hard work indeed.
And he finished on the very day a crafty, ravenous wolf arrived in the land…
Crunchy was asleep in his straw hut when a knock at the door suddenly woke him.
“Who's there?” he asked sleepily.
“I'm a kindly farmer, bringing snacks round to my neighbours,” came the reply.
“Oh, how lovely! I've been asleep so long that I'm hungry, squeak-squeak!” said the delighted little pig.
Crunchy jumped to his feet and opened the door. But there was no kindly farmer with a snack waiting outside. It was the crafty, ravenous wolf!

With a fierce look and a mouthful of enormous teeth, the wolf lunged straight at the small, sleepy pig. Luckily, Crunchy did not wait to end up in the intruder's tummy. He quickly slammed the door. The wolf was almost across the threshold when it caught him right on the nose! He howled in pain and sprang away from the house!
“You little pig!” he threatened Crunchy. “Open this door! You won't get away from me!”
Crunchy trembled with fear. “Not for anything in the world! You lied to me! You're no kindly farmer, and you certainly didn't come to bring me a snack!”
For a moment, all was quiet. Crunchy bitterly regretted not putting even one window in his house. “Oh, if only I had a window! Then I could see what that wolf is up to!”
Outside, the furious wolf prowled around the house, looking for the best way in. At last, he lost patience and shouted, “Enough! I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house down!”

The wolf puffed himself up like a balloon and blew a mighty gale from his lungs! The walls flew apart in every direction, and the straw roof fell to the ground right beside Crunchy! Squealing and squeaking with fright, the little pig ran for his brother's house!
And so the house built in one day fell apart with just one puff.
Oinky was still fishing when he saw Crunchy racing towards him.
“Brother, let's hide, squeak-squeak! The wolf is chasing me! He's terribly crafty and terribly hungry!” cried Crunchy.
Oinky did not need telling twice. Both pigs dashed into the wooden house and slammed the door behind them.
Only a few moments later, there was a knock at the door.
“Who's there?” asked the pigs.
“I'm a kindly farmer, bringing snacks round to my neighbours.”
But Oinky, warned by Crunchy, did not believe him. “You're very crafty, Mr Wolf, but you won't fool me. Enough lies! I can see your grey tail through the window!”

The wolf boiled with rage. “Open the door, you snuffling snouts! I'll get my paws on you and gobble you up!” Of course, this only made the pigs more certain that opening the door would be a very bad idea.

For a moment, all was quiet. Oinky peered through the window and saw the furious wolf prowling around the house, looking for a way in. At last, he lost patience and shouted, “Enough! I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house down!”
The wolf blew for the first time, and the walls of the house shook mightily.
The wolf blew for the second time, and planks and sticks began flying off the roof.
The wolf blew for the third time, and the whole house fell apart, crashing down on the pigs!
They squealed in terror and ran to their third brother's house.
And so the house built in three days fell apart with just three puffs.
Eusebius, who had just finished building, was washing his trotters in a trough beside the porch of his new house. Suddenly, he heard his brothers shouting:
“Brother, let's hide! The wolf is chasing us, squeak-squeak!”
Eusebius wasted no time. All three pigs dashed into the stone house and bolted the door behind them.
Only a few moments later, there was a knock at the door.
“Who's there?” asked the pigs.
“I'm a kindly farmer, bringing snacks round to my neighbours.”
But the pigs did not believe him. Eusebius answered firmly, “You're no farmer. You're a trickster, oink-oink! Go away, Wolf!”
The wolf flew into a rage again. “How much longer will you keep this up, you curly tails? Open this door! There's no escaping me!”

For a moment, all was quiet. The three pigs peered through the window and watched the furious wolf prowling around the house, looking for a way in. At last, he lost patience and shouted, “Enough! I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house down!”
The wolf took a deep breath and blew for the first time, but the house did not even tremble.
The wolf blew for the second time. Nothing happened!
The wolf blew for the third time, and the fourth, and the fifth… until he was tired and out of breath.

The stone house stood firm and undamaged. From inside, Eusebius called out teasingly, “Blow, Mr Wolf! Blow all you like! You'll run out of breath and drop with exhaustion, but you'll never blow down a house of stone! Oink-oink!”
Once again, all was quiet. Certain that the wolf was up to something, the pigs began to talk things over.
Crunchy said, “He can't come through the door, because we won't let him in.”
Oinky added, “He can't come through the window either. He'll get an oak shutter right on his nose.”
Eusebius clutched his head with his trotters. “Oh no, squeak-squeak! He'll try to come down the chimney! It's the only way in! We must light a fire!”
The pigs quickly lit a fire and hung a pot of water over the flames.
Eusebius was right. The pigs had only just got the fire going when they heard footsteps overhead. The wolf was walking across the roof towards the chimney!
A moment later, the tip of his tail and his hind paws appeared in the fireplace. Then suddenly, SPLASH! The wolf's bottom landed in the pot of hot water!
“Owww!” The wolf howled in pain and shot out of the chimney like a rocket! At the sight of him, Crunchy, Oinky, and Eusebius doubled over with laughter!
And so the house built with such care over more than three weeks saved the three little pigs!

Eusebius's hard work and care had saved him and his two brothers, Crunchy and Oinky, from the crafty, ravenous wolf. So remember: those who put care into their work can sleep soundly. The effort we make today brings good things to us and to those we love.

And the wolf? He had learnt his lesson and never showed his face in those parts again. Later, people said he had become a kindly farmer and really had started bringing snacks round to his neighbours. Can we believe that? You can decide for yourselves!
